chapter_title: Identification and Characterization of Problematic Soil and Rock

sections.title: Collapsible, Expansive, and Organic Soils
sections.summary: Collapsible soils (typically ML/CL, low plasticity) undergo sudden volume decrease upon wetting; collapse potential CP = ΔH/Ho × 100% from single-oedometer test. Expansive soils (Activity > 1, LL > 35%, PI > 20%) swell on wetting and shrink on drying; swell potential from oedometer swell tests; shrinkage limit test. Organic soils and peats have high water content (>100% possible), high primary and secondary compression (Cα/Cc ≈ 0.05 for most clays, higher for organics), and possible high corrosion risk. Field vane shear (VST) useful for non-fibrous organic soils; avoid in fibrous peat.
sections.body:
Collapsible soils: Typically non-plastic (ML or CL classification) with low dry density. Collapse is triggered by wetting under load. Identified by screening criteria including LI, dry density, porosity, and Atterberg limits (various methods). Collapse potential CP = ΔH/Ho × 100% from single-oedometer test at estimated overburden stress, inundated with water (Eq 5.2). Alternative double-oedometer method. Severity from Table 5-3. Commonly found in loess, alluvial fans, residual soils, and compacted fills dry of optimum. Hollow-stem auger suitable for sampling.

Expansive soils: Typically high-plasticity clays (CH) with Activity > 1, LL > 35–50%, PI > 20–35%. Swell and shrink in active zone (top 1–3 m typically). Identification screening: liquid limit, plasticity index, activity (Table 5-4, Seed et al. 1962; Table 5-5, Raman 1967; Table 5-6, Altmeyer 1955), free swell test. Direct characterization by one-dimensional swell test (swell potential = swell % at constant stress; swell pressure from reload test).

Organic soils and peats: Classification by ash content and moisture content per Landva et al. (1983) (Table 5-9). High water content (>100% possible), primary compressibility (Cc from consolidation tests), and significant secondary compression (Cα). Organic soils avoided or removed when possible. VST for undrained shear strength in non-fibrous organics; standard tests may not apply to fibrous peat.
key_points: Collapsible soils: ML/CL, low density; CP = ΔH/Ho × 100% at overburden stress when inundated
Expansive soils: Activity > 1, LL > 35%, PI > 20%; swell potential from one-dimensional swell/swell pressure tests
Shrinkage limit identifies lower bound of volume change; active zone typically top 1–3 m
Organic soils: high wn, high primary and secondary compression; avoid or remove before construction

sections.title: Dispersive, Liquefiable, and Colluvial Soils
sections.summary: Dispersive soils: high exchangeable sodium percentage (ESP) causes deflocculation in water, leading to internal erosion and piping; identified by Sherard et al. (1976) chart (TDS vs. ESP), pinhole test (ASTM D4647), and crumb test. Liquefiable soils: loose saturated cohesionless; susceptibility from SPT (N1)60 correction with CN = (pa/σ'vo)^0.5; CPT chart from Youd et al. (2001); Bq from CPTU. Colluvium/talus: heterogeneous granular deposits on slopes; test pits and trenches most suitable for characterization; compressibility from oedometer tests.
sections.body:
Dispersive soils: Exchangeable sodium ions in clay fraction cause dispersion in water, leading to piping and internal erosion in embankments and slopes. ESP = exchangeable sodium / CEC × 100%. Identified by: (1) Sherard et al. (1976) chart using total dissolved solids (TDS) and ESP; (2) pinhole dispersion test (ASTM D4647) — water passed through hole in soil specimen, turbidity and hole diameter classify dispersiveness (Table 5-11); (3) crumb test — soil placed in distilled water; (4) double hydrometer test. High dispersiveness: high sodium content, high LL, certain clay minerals. Treatment: add calcium ions (lime, gypsum) or mechanical compaction at higher moisture content.

Liquefiable soils: Loose, saturated coarse-grained soils; shear strain-induced excess pore pressure leads to near-zero effective stress and loss of strength. Liquefaction susceptibility screening: particle-size criteria (D50 < 2 mm, fines < 35%). SPT: (N1)60 = CN × N60 where CN = (pa/σ'vo)^0.5, limited to CN ≤ 1.7. CPT liquefaction resistance chart (Youd et al. 2001, Figure 5-20). Additional characterization of extent from soundings at regular intervals across site.

Colluvium and talus: Heterogeneous deposits formed by downslope movement and accumulation. Highly variable composition; potential for unstable conditions. Test pits and trenches most suitable for characterization. Compressibility from conventional consolidation tests.
key_points: Dispersive soils: identified by pinhole test (ASTM D4647), TDS-ESP chart, crumb test
Dispersive soils are particularly hazardous in embankment dam cores and slope fills
Liquefaction: (N1)60 = CN × N60; CN = (pa/σ'vo)^0.5; CPT chart from Youd et al. (2001)
Colluvium: heterogeneous, highly variable; test pits and trenches for characterization

sections.title: Degradable Rock, Corrosive Soils, and Other Problematic Materials
sections.summary: Degradable rock (shale, clay-shale, coal): characterized by slake durability index ID(2) and jar slake index. Table 5-12 provides shale suitability for rock fill (ID(2) > 85% and jar slake > 3 for good fill). Corrosive soils: high corrosion risk when resistivity < 2000 ohm-cm; also from acid soils, organic soils, and soils with high sulfate/chloride content. Sensitive clays: St = su,undisturbed/su,remolded; St > 4 moderate, >8 high, >50 quick; Norwegian quick clays with LI > 1. Sulfate-bearing soils: sulfate-induced heave when lime/cement applied to soils with >1,000 ppm sulfates. Permafrost: permanently frozen ground; thaw on warming causes dramatic strength loss and settlement.
sections.body:
Degradable rock: Shales, mudstones, and clay-shales may degrade rapidly when exposed to atmosphere. Classified by slake durability (ASTM D4644 — drum with wet steel rollers, ID(2) = mass retained after 2 cycles / initial mass × 100%) and jar slake index. Table 5-12: ID(2) > 90% and jar slake > 3 = low degradation potential; ID(2) < 75% or jar slake ≤ 1 = high degradation; requires special fill or disposal consideration.

Corrosive soils (Table 5-13): Acid soils (pH < 5.5), soil with organic matter, soils in permanently saturated zones, soils with high sulfate or chloride. Resistivity < 2000 ohm-cm indicates corrosion risk. American Water Works Association criteria rate corrosion potential from resistivity, pH, chloride, sulfate, and sulfide measurements.

Cemented sands: Stronger than uncemented; cementation from carbonates, silica, iron oxides. Potential problems: cementing agents may dissolve; cemented material may collapse when disturbed; potential to mislead classification from SPT or CPT.

Sensitive quick clays: St = su,undisturbed / su,remolded (at same water content). High sensitivity (St > 8) indicates large strength loss when disturbed; quick clays (St > 50) are particularly hazardous. LI > 1 indicates sensitivity risk. Norwegian quick clays have high sensitivity due to leaching of salt from marine clays. Thin-walled large-diameter samplers needed for highly sensitive soils.

Sulfate-bearing soils: Addition of lime, fly ash, or cement to soils with sulfate content > 1000 ppm can cause sulfate-induced heave. Test for sulfate content before specifying lime/cement treatment.

Permafrost: Permanently frozen for ≥ 2 consecutive years. Thaw on temperature increase causes dramatic settlement and strength loss. Identified by surface geomorphology (polygonal ground, stone nets, pingos, ice wedges). Core sampling required to assess ice content and structure.
key_points: Degradable rock (shale): slake durability ID(2) and jar slake index; ID(2) < 75% indicates high degradation
Corrosive soils: resistivity < 2000 ohm-cm indicates risk; also from pH, Cl, SO4, organic content
Sensitive quick clays: St = su,undisturbed/su,remolded; St > 50 = quick; LI > 1 indicates susceptibility
Sulfate-induced heave: do NOT use lime/cement on soils with >1000 ppm sulfate without testing
Permafrost: permanently frozen; thaw causes dramatic settlement; identified by surface geomorphology
